html:
French writer and thinker of the Enlightenment, born François-Marie Arouet in Paris in 1694. He attacked religious intolerance and the power of the church, and defended freedom of thought and speech.

He was sharp tongued from the start and was twice locked in the Bastille. Exiled to England from 1726 to 1728, he admired its freedoms, its tolerance and the science of Isaac Newton, and wrote Letters on the English to praise them, which got the book burned in France.

He wrote plays, histories, poems and thousands of letters. His short novel Candide (1759) mocks the idea that this is the best of all possible worlds, with the Lisbon earthquake as one of its blows. He spent years at the court of Frederick the Great and wrote to Catherine the Great. In his last decades he lived at Ferney near the Swiss border, where he campaigned to clear Jean Calas, a Protestant executed after an unjust trial.

He also wrote for the Encyclopédie. He died in Paris in 1778, eleven years before the French Revolution his ideas helped inspire.
